opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is infrastructure, and specifically how fast you can iterate.

People often assume the bottleneck is algorithms: a cleverer RL objective, a better reward model, some new trick. Those things matter, but in my experience they're rarely what limits progress. What limits progress is how quickly you can run an experiment, see the result, and decide what to try next. If one iteration of post-training takes a week, you get maybe fifty shots a year. If it takes a day, you get hundreds. The team with the faster loop usually wins, even with a less elegant idea.

RL for large models is especially hard here because the system is so heterogeneous. Pretraining is basically one big, very regular computation. RL has you generating rollouts with an inference engine, scoring them with reward models, verifiers, or environments, and then training, all with different hardware profiles and latency requirements. Weights have to move between these pieces, and data has to flow without stalls. Any one slow or buggy component drags down everything, so a lot of the real work is unglamorous engineering: making rollouts efficient, keeping the system stable, and making sure the numbers you see are actually correct.

Correctness matters more than people realize. In RL a subtle bug often doesn't crash anything. The reward still goes up, and the model just learns something slightly wrong, or you draw the wrong conclusion from an ablation. So good infrastructure isn't only about speed. It's about being able to trust your experiments.

The second bottleneck, closely related, is environments and signal. As models get stronger, the easy, verifiable tasks get saturated. The question becomes where the reward comes from for harder, longer-horizon, more open-ended work. Building rich environments and reliable evaluations at scale is becoming as important as the training algorithm itself.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: it's less about inventing the next algorithm and more about building systems, both infrastructure and environments, that let researchers iterate quickly and trust what they see.

r001.rationale: The response identifies infrastructure and experiment iteration speed as bottlenecks, but does not state that the bottleneck is the number of infrastructure problems fixed per unit time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I don't think the biggest bottleneck is the model architecture anymore, and I don't even think it's compute in the way people usually mean it. I think it's the environment and evaluation side, which is a very unglamorous answer.

Let me explain what I mean. When we were doing RL for games, the environment was basically free. You could run millions of steps, the reward was unambiguous, and you could reset at any time. That's why so much of that era was about squeezing throughput out of the pipeline. Now we're trying to apply RL to language models, and suddenly the environment is the hard part. The task might be "write code that passes these tests," or "solve this math problem," or "help this user over a twenty-turn conversation," and each of those has a different notion of what a step is, what a reset is, and what a reward is. Building that infrastructure so that it's fast, reproducible, and doesn't leak is a huge amount of engineering, and it's where I've seen most teams get stuck.

The second piece, which is tied to the first, is reward signal quality. For verifiable domains like math and code, we've made a lot of progress because you can check the answer. But the moment you move to things where "correct" is fuzzy, you're leaning on a reward model or on human preference data, and both of those are noisy and expensive. The model will happily find whatever shortcut the reward model is rewarding, and you only find out after you've burned a run. So I'd say the real bottleneck is: how do we generate dense, trustworthy signal at scale for tasks that aren't trivially checkable? That's partly a data problem, partly a systems problem, and partly a research problem, and it doesn't fit neatly into any one team.

And then on the systems side, the thing that keeps me up at night is that training and inference are becoming the same workload. In post-training with RL you're generating rollouts with the model, scoring them, and then updating the weights, and you want all of that to happen in a loop with minimal idle time. The inference engines are optimized for one thing, the training frameworks are optimized for another, and gluing them together without stalling the GPUs is surprisingly hard. The best labs have spent years on this and it's still not solved cleanly.

So if I had to pick one word, I'd say "environments," but what I really mean is the whole loop around the model, not the model itself. The model will keep getting better. The question is whether we can build the loop that lets it get better on the things we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response names environments and evaluation infrastructure as the biggest bottleneck, but does not identify infrastructure repair throughput or the number of infrastructure problems fixed per unit time.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is getting a reliable learning signal. In pre-training, you have a relatively straightforward objective: predict the next token. In reinforcement learning and post-training, you have to decide what a good answer or a successful action actually means—and whether you can measure it accurately.

For coding or math, you can often check the result. But if you want a model to do research, carry out a long task, or help someone make a decision, evaluation becomes much harder. The outcome might be delayed, there may be multiple good answers, and your reward can accidentally encourage behavior that looks successful without actually being useful.

So I’d put a lot of emphasis on environments, feedback, and evaluation. More compute lets you generate more attempts, but you still need a way to tell which attempts represent real progress. And for long tasks, you need to figure out which decisions along the way deserve credit. I think that’s where a lot of the hard work will be.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies reliable learning signals, feedback, and evaluation as the bottleneck. It does not identify infrastructure repair throughput or the number of infrastructure problems fixed per unit time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is getting a reliable learning signal. Pre-training gives you a fairly straightforward objective: predict the next token. In post-training, especially with reinforcement learning, you have to decide what a good outcome actually is and how to measure it.

For something like coding, you can run tests, so you have a relatively clear signal. But if you want a model to do research or carry out a task that takes hours, success is much harder to verify. And even when you can measure the final outcome, it’s hard to tell which decisions along the way deserve credit.

So I think the challenge is building environments and feedback mechanisms that let models learn from meaningful experience. More compute helps, but if the reward is a poor proxy for what you want, you can spend a lot of compute teaching the wrong behavior.

r001.rationale: The response names obtaining reliable learning signals and verifying outcomes as the bottleneck. It does not identify infrastructure repair throughput or problems fixed per unit time.
